    Chapter summaries

    Ch 1, 3

    The problem

    What an agent, a reward, a return and a value are.

    01 · Ch 3

    Learning from a loop of rewards

    TL;DRThe agent acts, the world answers with a new state and a reward, and the agent’s goal is a large long-run sum of rewards.

    • No teacher names the right action; only rewards say how well it went.
    • Actions change later states, so credit for a reward must travel back in time.
    • The discount rate γ makes near rewards count more than far ones.

    In words: The return is the next reward plus every later reward, each shrunk by γ once per step.

    Remember: The reward says what to achieve, not how to achieve it.

    §3.1–3.3 · Eq 3.8
    02 · Ch 3

    Values and the Bellman equation

    TL;DRA state’s value vπ(s) is the expected return from s under π; it equals the expected reward plus the discounted value of the next state.

    • π weights the actions; the dynamics p weight next states and rewards.
    • Each value is written in terms of the values of its successors.
    • The optimal value v* takes the best action instead of π’s average.

    In words: Average over actions and outcomes of the reward plus the discounted value of where you land.

    Remember: A value predicts the return, and it is computed one step ahead.

    §3.5–3.6 · Eq 3.14 Illustrative

    Part I · Ch 2–8

    Tabular methods

    Small problems where every state or action has its own table entry.

    03 · Ch 2

    Explore or exploit

    TL;DREach action has an unknown value; always taking the best-looking one can lock onto a poor arm, so ε-greedy explores now and then.

    • The estimate Qₙ is the average of the rewards received so far.
    • Greedy exploits what it knows; ε-greedy picks a random action with probability ε.
    • On the 10-armed testbed, greedy found the best arm in only about one-third of tasks.

    In words: Move the estimate toward the newest reward by one n-th of the gap.

    Remember: NewEstimate ← OldEstimate + StepSize [Target − OldEstimate], the book’s pattern.

    Ch 2 · Eq 2.3 Illustrative
    04 · Ch 4

    Dynamic programming: sweep a known model

    TL;DRWith a perfect model p, dynamic programming sweeps every state, backing up values from successors, and alternates evaluation with greedy improvement until reaching v* and π*.

    • Value iteration folds one sweep of evaluation and the max into one update.
    • Greedy improvement never makes a policy worse: the policy improvement theorem.
    • Generalized policy iteration: evaluation and improvement pull toward one optimum.

    In words: Each sweep sets a state’s value to its best one-step lookahead using the old values.

    Remember: Dynamic programming needs the full model; later chapters learn without one.

    Ch 4 · Eq 4.10 Illustrative
    05 · Ch 5

    Monte Carlo: learn from whole episodes

    TL;DRMonte Carlo methods need no model: they play an episode to the end, compute the actual return, and move each visited state’s value toward it.

    • No bootstrapping: the target is the real return Gₜ.
    • Updates wait until the episode ends, so tasks must be episodic.
    • Exploration is kept up by exploring starts or ε-soft policies.

    In words: Move the state’s value a fraction α of the way toward the return that actually followed.

    Remember: Monte Carlo averages real returns and waits for the episode to end.

    Ch 5 · Eq 6.1 (§6.1) Illustrative
    06 · §6.1–6.3

    TD learning: a guess from a guess

    TL;DRTD learning updates after one step, using the reward plus the discounted estimate of the next state as its target: it bootstraps, without a model.

    • The TD error δₜ is the target minus the current estimate.
    • No waiting for the episode to end, so it learns online.
    • On the random walk, TD(0) learned faster than constant-α Monte Carlo.

    In words: Move the value toward one real reward plus the discounted estimate of the next state.

    Remember: Monte Carlo targets Gₜ; TD targets Rₜ₊₁ + γV(Sₜ₊₁).

    §6.1–6.3 · Eq 6.2 Illustrative
    07 · §6.4–6.5

    Sarsa or Q-learning: the cliff

    TL;DRSarsa learns the values of the ε-greedy policy it follows; Q-learning learns the optimal policy’s values whatever it follows, so on the cliff it walks the edge.

    • Sarsa is on-policy: its target uses the next action it actually takes.
    • Q-learning is off-policy: its target takes the max over next actions.
    • Exploring on the edge sometimes falls, so Q-learning’s online reward is lower.

    In words: Move the action value toward the reward plus the discounted value of the best next action.

    Remember: Sarsa takes the safer path while exploring; Q-learning takes the optimal one.

    Example 6.6 · Eq 6.8
    08 · Ch 7

    n-step: from TD to Monte Carlo

    TL;DRn-step methods add up n real rewards and then bootstrap from the estimated value; n = 1 is one-step TD and a whole episode is Monte Carlo.

    • Longer backups wait longer but rely less on current estimates.
    • On the random walk, an intermediate n learned best (Figure 7.2).
    • The same return gives n-step Sarsa and off-policy versions.

    In words: n real rewards, discounted, then the current estimate of the state reached after n steps.

    Remember: n sets how far to look ahead before trusting the estimate.

    Ch 7 · Eq 7.1
    09 · Ch 8

    Planning with a model: Dyna

    TL;DRDyna-Q learns a model from real experience and replays imagined transitions from it, so each real step feeds many planning updates and values spread faster.

    • Direct RL and planning use the same Q-learning update.
    • In the Dyna maze, 50 planning steps reached a good policy in three episodes.
    • A wrong model misleads planning until experience corrects it.

    Remember: Learning and planning differ only in where their experience comes from.

    Ch 8 · §8.2 Illustrative

    Part II · Ch 9–13

    Approximate methods

    Weights stand in for the table, so learning generalizes.

    10 · Ch 9

    Generalize with weights

    TL;DRWhen states are too many for a table, v̂(s,w) uses a weight vector w shared across states, so an SGD step on one state also changes similar states.

    • Features x(s) describe states; linear methods use v̂ = wᵀx(s).
    • Semi-gradient TD bootstraps, so it is not a true gradient method.
    • State aggregation gives one weight per group of states (Figure 9.1).

    In words: Nudge the weights along the gradient, by the error between the target Uₜ and the estimate.

    Remember: Update one state and its neighbors change too: that is generalization.

    Ch 9 · Eq 9.7 Illustrative
    11 · Ch 10–11

    Control with approximation, and the deadly triad

    TL;DRSemi-gradient Sarsa learns control with approximation, as on Mountain Car; but approximation, bootstrapping and off-policy training together can make the weights diverge.

    • Mountain Car: the car must first back away to build momentum.
    • The danger is not due to control: prediction alone can diverge.
    • Baird’s counterexample: off-policy semi-gradient TD weights grow without bound.

    Remember: With any two of the three, instability can be avoided.

    Example 10.1 · §11.2–11.3 Illustrative
    12 · Ch 12

    Eligibility traces: credit the recent past

    TL;DRAn eligibility trace zₜ marks recently visited states and fades by γλ each step; each TD error then updates all of them at once, in proportion to their traces.

    • λ = 0 gives one-step TD; λ = 1 behaves like Monte Carlo.
    • The TD error δₜ (12.6) is spread back through the trace z.
    • One trace vector replaces storing the last n feature vectors.

    In words: Fade the old trace by γλ, then add the gradient of the current state’s value.

    Remember: The trace is short-term memory; the weights are long-term memory.

    Ch 12 · Eq 12.5–12.6 Illustrative
    13 · Ch 13

    Learn the policy directly

    TL;DRPolicy-gradient methods adjust policy parameters θ so actions followed by high returns become more likely; actor–critic adds a learned critic to cut variance.

    • The policy can stay stochastic and can approach a deterministic one.
    • REINFORCE uses the full return Gₜ, so it is a Monte Carlo method.
    • Actor–critic replaces Gₜ with the critic’s TD error δₜ.

    In words: Push θ to make the action taken more likely, scaled by its return, divided by its probability.

    Remember: Value methods act from values; policy methods learn the choice itself.

    Ch 13 · Eq 13.8 Illustrative

    Part III · Ch 14–17

    Looking deeper

    Brains, case studies and the open problems.

    14 · Ch 14–15

    Brains and behavior

    TL;DRAnimal learning and dopamine neurons match reinforcement learning closely: the phasic activity of dopamine neurons behaves like the TD error, a reward prediction error.

    • Classical conditioning corresponds to prediction; instrumental conditioning to control.
    • After learning, the dopamine burst moves from the reward to the earliest predicting cue.
    • When an expected reward is omitted, activity drops below baseline.

    In words: The reward plus the discounted next estimate, minus the current estimate.

    Remember: Dopamine signals a reward prediction error, not the reward itself.

    §15.3–15.6 · Eq 6.5 Illustrative
    15 · Ch 16–17

    Case studies and frontiers

    TL;DRThe book’s case studies, from TD-Gammon to AlphaGo, combine its core ideas with function approximation; Chapter 17 names the open problems ahead.

    • TD-Gammon learned backgammon by self-play with TD(λ) and a neural network.
    • The deep Q-network learned Atari games from pixels with Q-learning.
    • Frontiers: general value functions, options, state from observations, reward design.

    Remember: Every case study reuses the book’s core update rules.

    Ch 16 · Ch 17
    16 · Recap

    Recap: the whole book in one picture

    TL;DRPart I’s methods differ in the width and depth of their updates: TD, dynamic programming, Monte Carlo and exhaustive search sit at the corners.

    • Width: sample updates (one trajectory) or expected updates (every possibility).
    • Depth: one-step bootstrapping to full returns; n-step and λ lie between.
    • A third dimension, on-policy or off-policy, runs perpendicular to the page.

    Remember: Every method nudges an estimate toward a target; only the target changes.

    Figure 8.11 · §8.13

    Check yourself

    What changed?

    Three methods from the lineage map, each one change away from its parent. Pick what changed.

    1Q-learning grew out of Sarsa (§6.5). What changed in its update?

    Sarsa uses Q(Sₜ₊₁, Aₜ₊₁) of the action actually taken; Q-learning uses maxₐ Q(Sₜ₊₁, a), so it learns q* whatever the behavior policy (6.8).

    2TD(0) grew out of constant-α Monte Carlo (§6.1). What changed?

    Constant-α MC (6.1) waits for Gₜ; TD(0) (6.2) bootstraps from the estimate of the next state, so it learns every step.

    3What did REINFORCE with baseline (§13.4) add to REINFORCE?

    Subtracting a baseline (13.11) leaves the expected update unchanged but can reduce its variance a lot.

    ← Topic ExplorerNext: Compare →

    Check yourself

    Tell them apart

    Three questions that separate methods by the properties in the master table.

    1On Cliff Walking (Example 6.6), which method learns the safer path while it explores with ε-greedy?

    Sarsa is on-policy: it learns the values of the ε-greedy policy it follows, so it keeps away from the cliff. Q-learning learns the optimal path along the edge.

    2Which of these needs a perfect model of the environment’s dynamics?

    Dynamic programming (Chapter 4) assumes the dynamics p(s′, r | s, a) are known; TD and Monte Carlo learn from experience.

    3Which method does not bootstrap?

    Monte Carlo updates toward complete sampled returns; Sarsa and Dyna-Q update toward targets built from current estimates.
